source.title: Flatness is Necessary, Neural Collapse is Not: Rethinking Generalization via Grokking
source.authors: Ting-Xu Han; Linara Adilova; Henning Petzka; J. Kleesiek; Michael Kamp

record.tranche_reason: The paper follows the original modular-arithmetic grokking setup and measures the delayed training/validation accuracy pattern, while also tracking geometric quantities.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own modular-arithmetic grokking result. It also reports delayed generalization deliberately induced with a relative-flatness regularizer on image and text tasks; those induced results are recorded as findings with no matching version, not as evidence that grokking arises without that intervention. Prior-work results cited in the paper are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper reruns the Power et al. modular-arithmetic setup (2-layer transformer, AdamW, weight decay 1.0, 50/50 split, three seeds). Its Figure 1 shows its own train and validation accuracy curves with delayed generalization, which bears on V1. The test is qualitative: grokking is used mainly as a probe for flatness and neural-collapse measures. All other delayed-generalization results are deliberately induced by a sharpness-promoting regularizer, so they bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that relative flatness is potentially necessary for generalization and neural collapse is not; that collapse leads to flatness under classical assumptions; and that regularizing away flatness induces grokking-like delays. They also caution that it is unclear whether these artificially induced phases mirror the mechanisms of standard grokking.
record.recipe_differences: The paper says it follows the original modular-arithmetic setup and reports a 2-layer transformer, AdamW, learning rate 10−4, weight decay 1.0, 106 steps and a 50/50 train/validation split; it adds geometric measurements and averages over three seeds.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative-flatness regularizer's outcomes vary with regularization strength and weight cap; the paper reports instability at stronger settings and little effect at weaker settings. For induced recovery, regularizer removal is accompanied by learning-rate, schedule and weight-decay changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Maximizing relative sharpness keeps validation accuracy low (CIFAR-10 ~60% vs ~78%; ImageNet-100 ~38% vs ~43%; SST-5 ~37-38% vs ~44-45%) while train accuracy nears 100%. Validation accuracy rises after the regularizer is removed and the optimizer settings are changed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Penalizing relative flatness deliberately induces grokking-like delayed generalization in ResNets, ViTs and fine-tuned small language models.

fits_no_version.finding: In modular-arithmetic grokking, neural-collapse clustering (NCC) falls during memorization, before generalization. Relative flatness stays high and drops sharply only at generalization onset. Representativeness improves with the initial rise in validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Penultimate-layer geometric measures track grokking: clustering precedes generalization, while flatness coincides with its onset.

record.problems: The modular-arithmetic result is described in text and a figure without numerical accuracy values in the prose; the paper does not test training-set-size dependence. The paper reports three-seed averages for the grokking experiment, but does not give numerical uncertainty estimates there. The induced recovery experiments change additional training settings when the regularizer is removed, so the recovery is not isolated to removal alone. Section 6 names ResNet-10 for CIFAR-10, while Appendix C.2 describes ResNet-18.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results relevant to the listed claim versions were left out. NCC suppression and other flatness measurements concern the paper's neural-collapse/flatness claims, not a measured claim-version outcome about grokking mechanisms.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size: only a 50/50 split is run. Quantitative chance-to-near-perfect values are not reported in text.
No circuit or Fourier-mechanism analysis and no memorization-removal measures.
No naturally arising delays on non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation; the image and text delays are induced.
No natural grokking in LLM pretraining or fine-tuning; the SST-5 delays are induced by the regularizer.
No weight-decay, critical-dataset-size or ungrokking tests.
No comparison of algorithms across runs.

missing.what: Timing of NCC, relative flatness and representativeness relative to the validation-accuracy jump in modular-arithmetic grokking. These are continuous measures, but not circuit measures, so they do not directly bear on V2.

record.verdict_notes: The grokking replication is a means to an end; the paper's focus is flatness versus neural collapse. The V1 support is therefore weak and qualitative. The checklist says three-seed means and spreads are plotted. All non-algorithmic delays are intervention-induced and excluded from V3 and V4. There are minor internal inconsistencies: ResNet-10 vs ResNet-18, and a 42% vs 43% ViT baseline.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not vary training-set size, so it does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.
It does not measure formation of a generalizing circuit, memorizing components being removed, or circuit progress measures anticipating the accuracy jump.

The non-algorithmic delayed-generalization results are deliberately induced by regularization. The paper does not test naturally arising delays or initialization-scale/weight-norm lazy-to-rich transitions.
The language-model results are deliberately induced during SST-5 fine-tuning; the paper does not test naturally occurring grokking in realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
It does not test the low-norm efficiency account, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.
It does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
It does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts explain the delay.

rows.subject: 2-layer transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained on symbolic algorithmic tasks, following the original setup.

conditions.value: modular arithmetic (e.g., x + y mod p)

rows.measure: Training and validation accuracy over training
rows.value: The paper describes memorization with zero generalization for an extended period, followed by sudden generalization with high accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over three seeds; numerical error bars not stated in the text.
rows.note: The paper describes the delayed accuracy pattern, but does not state a numerical chance-level starting accuracy or a numerical training-accuracy saturation value here.
rows.check: The link and state are right, but the value is only a qualitative description of Figure 1. No chance-level start, final validation accuracy or delay length is given in text. Train fraction is fixed at 50%, so the dataset-size part of V1 cannot be read.

rows.subject: ResNet-10 (Section 6; ResNet-18 in Appendix C)
rows.operation_detail: Compared standard CIFAR-10 training with training under a relative-flatness regularizer maintained throughout training.
rows.note: This delayed-generalization behavior is deliberately induced by the regularizer.
rows.check: The architecture is inconsistent within the paper: Section 6 says ResNet-10, while the Figure 4 caption and Appendix C.2 say ResNet-18. The ~60% vs ~78% gap is deliberately induced by the regularizer and is not evidence on any version.

relationships.condition: 2-layer transformer, modular arithmetic, original Power et al. recipe, 50/50 split, 3 seeds
relationships.reason: R1: Figure 1 shows train accuracy saturating early and validation accuracy jumping much later. The evidence is qualitative and from a single train fraction.
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy saturated early and validation accuracy jumped much later.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
